Chapters 1–3 develop the language needed to describe limiting behaviour precisely. We begin with sets, functions and distance on the real line. We then use distance to say what it means for a sequence or a function to approach a limit, before bringing these ideas together in the definition of continuity. No previous experience of rigorous limit proofs is assumed.

The formal definitions matter, but they are not intended to replace intuition. Each definition will be translated into ordinary language and followed by examples. In particular, we shall repeatedly ask which quantities may depend on a prescribed tolerance and which quantities must work uniformly after they have been chosen.

Chapter 1
Sets, Functions and the Real Line

Calculus studies functions of real numbers, so we first need precise language for describing collections of numbers and regions of the real line. This language will also allow us to express “closeness” using inequalities.

1.1 Sets and set notation

A set is a collection of objects. If an object x belongs to a set A, we write x ∈ A; otherwise we write x∉A. The empty set, which has no elements, is denoted by ∅.

Definition 1.1 (Subset and proper subset). Let A and B be sets. We write A ⊆ B if every element of A is also an element of B. We write A ⊊ B if A ⊆ B and A≠B.

The symbols ∈ and ⊆ describe different relationships. For example, 1 ∈{1,2} is a statement about an element, while {1,2}⊆{1,2,3} is a statement about two sets. In particular, it would be incorrect to replace either symbol by the other.

Two sets are equal exactly when they contain the same elements. Thus a useful method for proving A = B is to prove both A ⊆ B and B ⊆ A.

Definition 1.2 (Basic set operations). Let A and B be subsets of a set X. Their union, intersection and set difference are

A ∪ B = {x ∈ X : x ∈ A or x ∈ B}, A ∩ B = {x ∈ X : x ∈ A and x ∈ B}, A ∖ B = {x ∈ A : x∉B}.

The sets A and B are disjoint if A ∩ B = ∅.

The colon in set-builder notation means “such that”. For instance, if X = {−2,−1,0,1,2,3}, then

{x ∈ X : −2 ≤ x < 3} = {−2,−1,0,1,2}.

Example 1.3. Let A = {1,2,3} and B = {2,4}. Reading directly from the definitions gives

A ∪ B = {1,2,3,4}, A ∩ B = {2}, A ∖ B = {1,3}.

The order and repetition of entries do not matter in a set, so, for example, {1,2,2} = {2,1}.

When every set under discussion is a subset of one fixed set X, the set difference X ∖ A is called the complement of A in X. The notation Ac is also common when X is clear from the context, but X ∖ A records the set from which the elements of A are removed. Complements convert unions into intersections, and intersections into unions.

Proposition 1.4 (De Morgan’s laws). Let A and B be subsets of a set X. Then

X ∖ (A ∪ B) = (X ∖ A) ∩ (X ∖ B), X ∖ (A ∩ B) = (X ∖ A) ∪ (X ∖ B).

Proof. We prove the first identity by showing that both sides contain exactly the same elements. For x ∈ X, the definitions of complement, union and intersection give

x ∈ X ∖ (A ∪ B) ⟺x∉A ∪ B ⟺x∉A and x∉B ⟺x ∈ X ∖ A and x ∈ X ∖ B ⟺x ∈ (X ∖ A) ∩ (X ∖ B).

The second equivalence holds because x fails to belong to A ∪ B exactly when it belongs to neither set. The second identity is proved in the same way, using the fact that x∉A ∩ B exactly when x∉A or x∉B. □

Sets are unordered, so {1,2} = {2,1}. To record order we use ordered pairs: (a,b) = (c,d) means exactly that a = c and b = d. Thus (1,2)≠(2,1).

Definition 1.5 (Cartesian product). Let A and B be sets. Their Cartesian product is the set of ordered pairs

A × B = {(a,b) : a ∈ A and b ∈ B}.

For example,

{1,2}×{0,5} = {(1,0),(1,5),(2,0),(2,5)}.

The plane is ℝ2 = ℝ × ℝ, whose elements (x,y) are pairs of real coordinates. Round brackets are also used for open intervals below; the context always shows whether (a,b) denotes a pair or an interval.

Exercise 1.6 (Complements and products). Let X = {1,2,3,4,5,6}, A = {1,2,3} and B = {2,4,6}.

  1. Find X ∖ (A ∪ B) and (X ∖ A) ∩ (X ∖ B), and check that they agree.
  2. Prove the second of De Morgan’s laws by the method used for the first.
  3. List the elements of {0,1}×{2,3,4}. Explain why this set is not equal to {2,3,4}×{0,1}, although both sets have six elements.

1.2 Number systems and intervals

The number systems used here form a nested collection of increasingly large sets. We write

ℕ = {0,1,2,…},ℤ+ = {1,2,3,…},

and

ℤ = {…,−2,−1,0,1,2,…},ℚ,ℝ.

Here ℚ is the set of rational numbers and ℝ is the set of real numbers. Notice that 0 ∈ ℕ but 0∉ℤ+.

These sets satisfy

ℤ+ ⊊ ℕ ⊊ ℤ ⊊ ℚ ⊊ ℝ.

Intervals describe sets of real numbers lying between endpoints. If a,b ∈ ℝ and a < b, then

(a,b) = {x ∈ ℝ : a < x < b}, [a,b] = {x ∈ ℝ : a ≤ x ≤ b}, [a,b) = {x ∈ ℝ : a ≤ x < b}, (a,b] = {x ∈ ℝ : a < x ≤ b}.

Round brackets exclude an endpoint and square brackets include it. Thus a∉(a,b) but a ∈ [a,b].

Infinite intervals include

(−∞,a),(−∞,a],(a,∞),[a,∞).

The symbols ∞ and −∞ are not real numbers, so an infinite endpoint is never included and always receives a round bracket.

Figure 1.1 summarises the four finite interval types. An open circle excludes an endpoint, whereas a filled circle includes it.

Example 1.7 (Translating an inequality). The conditions − 2 < x and x ≤ 3 must both hold. Hence

{x ∈ ℝ : −2 < x ≤ 3} = (−2,3].

The left endpoint is excluded because the first inequality is strict, whereas the right endpoint is included.

Example 1.8 (Combining intervals). The intersection contains only points lying in both intervals, whereas the union contains points lying in at least one. Therefore

(1,4] ∩ [3,6) = [3,4], (1,4] ∪ [3,6) = (1,6).

1.3 Boundedness, maxima and minima

An upper bound need not be a member of the set it bounds. This distinction is important now and will reappear when integration is defined later in the course.

Definition 1.9 (Bounds). Let A ⊆ ℝ be nonempty.

  • A number M ∈ ℝ is an upper bound of A if x ≤ M for every x ∈ A.
  • A number m ∈ ℝ is a lower bound of A if m ≤ x for every x ∈ A.
  • The set A is bounded above if it has an upper bound, bounded below if it has a lower bound, and bounded if both conditions hold.

In symbols, boundedness above has the quantifier structure

∃ ⁡M ∈ ℝ∀ ⁡x ∈ A : x ≤ M.

The symbol ∃ ⁡ means “there exists” and ∀ ⁡ means “for every”. Their order matters: one number M must work for every element x of the set.

Definition 1.10 (Maximum and minimum). Let A ⊆ ℝ be nonempty. A number M is the maximum of A if M ∈ A and x ≤ M for every x ∈ A. A number m is the minimum of A if m ∈ A and m ≤ x for every x ∈ A.

Thus a maximum is an upper bound that is actually attained. A set can have many upper bounds, but it can have at most one maximum.

The definitions above distinguish being bounded from actually attaining a bound. There is a third possibility that will be useful later: a set may have a best possible upper bound without containing it.

1.4 Supremum and infimum

Definition 1.11 (Supremum and infimum). Let A ⊆ ℝ be nonempty.

  • If A is bounded above, its supremum sup ⁡ A is its least upper bound: it is an upper bound, and it is no larger than any other upper bound.
  • If A is bounded below, its infimum inf ⁡ A is its greatest lower bound: it is a lower bound, and it is no smaller than any other lower bound.

Unlike a maximum or minimum, a supremum or infimum need not belong to the set.

Example 1.12 (Attained and non-attained bounds). Let

A = (0,1)andB = [0,1].

Every number at least 1 is an upper bound of either set, and every number at most 0 is a lower bound. The least and greatest of these bounds are

sup ⁡ A = sup ⁡ B = 1andinf ⁡ A = inf ⁡ B = 0.

To see that no number u < 1 is an upper bound, note that (max ⁡ {u,0} + 1)∕2 lies in both sets and exceeds u. Similarly, for ℓ > 0 the number min ⁡ {ℓ,1}∕2 lies in both sets and is smaller than ℓ, so no number ℓ > 0 is a lower bound. The set B contains its endpoints, so max ⁡ B = 1 and min ⁡ B = 0. The set A contains neither endpoint. Given any x ∈ A, the number (x + 1)∕2 is still in A and is larger than x, so A has no maximum. Similarly, x∕2 ∈ A is smaller than x, so A has no minimum. Figure 1.2 shows why the same best bounds can have different attainment in the two sets.

The Archimedean property says that, however large a real number is, there is a positive integer larger than it. We shall use this standard property when choosing an index in a limit proof. The following example also uses it to identify a supremum.

Example 1.13 (A discrete set without a maximum). Consider

C = {1 − 1 n : n ∈ ℤ+} = {0, 1 2, 2 3, 3 4,…}.

Every element of C is less than 1, so 1 is an upper bound. If u < 1, the Archimedean property of the real numbers allows us to choose n ∈ ℤ+ with n > 1∕(1 − u). Then

n > 1 1 − u 1 n < 1 − u 1 − 1 n > u.

The second line takes reciprocals of positive numbers, which reverses the inequality. The third adds u − 1∕n to both sides. Thus no number below 1 is an upper bound, and sup ⁡ C = 1. The value 1 is not in C, so C has no maximum. Its minimum is 0, attained when n = 1.

The deeper least-upper-bound property of ℝ guarantees that every nonempty set bounded above has a supremum, but its proof and systematic development are outside the present scope.

Example 1.14 (A set defined by an inequality). Let

E = {x ∈ ℝ : x2 < 4}.

Solving the inequality gives − 2 < x < 2, so E = (−2,2). Therefore E is bounded,

inf ⁡ E = −2andsup ⁡ E = 2,

but E has neither a minimum nor a maximum.

1.5 Absolute value and distance

For x ∈ ℝ, the absolute value is

|x| = { x, x ≥ 0, −x,x < 0.

It measures the distance from x to 0. More generally, the Euclidean distance between x,y ∈ ℝ is

d(x,y) = |x − y|.

If r > 0, saying that x is within distance r of a centre a means

|x − a| < r ⟺ − r < x − a < r ⟺a − r < x < a + r ⟺x ∈ (a − r,a + r).

The first equivalence uses the definition of absolute value. The second adds a to all three parts of the inequality. This description of a small interval around a point will be central to limits.

Example 1.15 (A distance inequality). To solve |x − 2| < 3, we translate the absolute value into a double inequality:

|x − 2| < 3 ⟺ − 3 < x − 2 < 3 ⟺ − 1 < x < 5.

Thus the solution set is (−1,5): the points whose distance from 2 is less than 3. Figure 1.3 displays the two parts of this geometric description.

Example 1.16 (A non-strict inequality). We solve |2x + 1|≤ 5 one operation at a time:

|2x + 1|≤ 5 ⟺ − 5 ≤ 2x + 1 ≤ 5 ⟺ − 6 ≤ 2x ≤ 4 ⟺ − 3 ≤ x ≤ 2.

We first removed the absolute value, then subtracted 1, and finally divided by the positive number 2, which preserved the inequality directions.

The most useful estimate involving absolute value is the triangle inequality.

Proposition 1.17 (Triangle inequality). For all x,y ∈ ℝ,

|x + y|≤|x| + |y|. (1.1)

Proof. The inequalities −|x|≤ x ≤|x| and −|y|≤ y ≤|y| follow from the definition of absolute value. Adding the corresponding parts gives

−|x|−|y| ≤ x + y, x + y ≤|x| + |y|.

Together these say

−(|x| + |y|) ≤ x + y ≤|x| + |y|.

By the definition of absolute value, this is equivalent to (1.1). □

Applying the triangle inequality to (x − y) + (y − z) = x − z gives its distance form.

Corollary 1.18 (Distance triangle inequality). For all x,y,z ∈ ℝ,

|x − z| = |(x − y) + (y − z)| ≤|x − y| + |y − z|.

Geometrically, travelling directly from x to z cannot be longer than travelling from x to y and then from y to z.

Rearranging the triangle inequality also gives a lower bound for a distance. This form will be used when we need to keep a quantity away from zero.

Corollary 1.19 (Reverse triangle inequality). For all x,y ∈ ℝ,

||x|−|y|| ≤|x − y|.

Proof. Applying the triangle inequality to x = (x − y) + y, and then subtracting |y|, gives

|x| ≤|x − y| + |y| |x|−|y| ≤|x − y|.

Exchanging the roles of x and y, and using |y − x| = |x − y|, gives |y|−|x|≤|x − y|. The number ||x|−|y|| equals either |x|−|y| or |y|−|x|, and both are at most |x − y|. □

Remark 1.20 (A common error). The triangle inequality is an inequality, not usually an equality. For example,

|1 + (−1)| = 0 < 2 = |1| + |− 1|.

Exercise 1.21 (Foundations consolidation). Let A = [−1,3) and B = (1,5].

  1. Find A ∩ B, A ∪ B and A ∖ B.
  2. State inf ⁡ A and sup ⁡ A, and decide whether A has a minimum or maximum.
  3. Rewrite |x − 1|≤ 2 as an interval and explain its geometric meaning.

The idea of distance now gives us a natural bridge from sets of numbers to functions: a function assigns an output to each allowed input, and limits will ask how distances between inputs control distances between outputs.

A formula such as x2 does not by itself specify a function. We must also say which inputs are allowed and in which set the outputs are being considered. These choices determine whether the function has properties such as injectivity or surjectivity.

1.6 Functions, images, preimages and composition

Definition 1.22 (Function). A function

f : A → B

assigns to every x ∈ A exactly one value f(x) ∈ B. The set A is the domain, the set B is the codomain, and x↦f(x) describes the rule of the function.

The requirement “exactly one” means that an input cannot be left without an output and cannot be assigned two different outputs. Different inputs are allowed to have the same output.

Once the domain, codomain and rule have been fixed, we can ask which outputs arise from a collection of inputs and which inputs lead into a collection of outputs.

Definition 1.23 (Image and preimage). Let f : A → B.

  • The image or range of f is

    f(A) = {f(x) : x ∈ A}.

  • If E ⊆ A, its image is

    f(E) = {f(x) : x ∈ E}.

  • If F ⊆ B, its preimage is

    f−1(F) = {x ∈ A : f(x) ∈ F}.

The image f(A) is always a subset of the codomain B, but it need not equal B. A preimage asks which inputs land in a chosen set of outputs. The notation f−1(F) is valid even when there is no inverse function.

Figure 1.4 gives a finite example of the distinction between codomain and image. The value 2 belongs to the specified codomain, but no input is mapped to it.

Example 1.24 (Image and preimage). Let f : ℝ → ℝ be defined by f(x) = x2. For E = [−2,1], the smallest squared value is 0 and the largest is 4, so

f(E) = [0,4].

For F = [0,4], a real number belongs to the preimage precisely when its square lies between 0 and 4:

f−1(F) = {x ∈ ℝ : 0 ≤ x2 ≤ 4} = [−2,2].

Notice that f(E) and f−1(F) happen to be intervals here, but they answer different questions.

Exercise 1.25 (Images of unions and intersections). Let f : A → B, and let E,F ⊆ A.

  1. Prove that

    f(E ∪ F) = f(E) ∪ f(F).

  2. Prove that

    f(E ∩ F) ⊆ f(E) ∩ f(F).
  3. Show by an example that equality need not hold in the second part.

Functions can be joined by feeding the output of one into another.

Definition 1.26 (Composition). Let f : A → B and g : B → C. Their composition g ∘ f : A → C is defined by

(g ∘ f)(x) = g(f(x)).

The function f acts first and g acts second.

Example 1.27 (Composition and its domain). Consider the rules

f(u) = uandg(x) = x − 1.

The composite expression is

(f ∘ g)(x) = x − 1.

For real-valued functions, the input to the square root must be non-negative. We therefore require

x − 1 ≥ 0 x ≥ 1.

The natural real domain of this composite is [1,∞).

Exercise 1.28 (Order of composition). Let f,g : ℝ → ℝ be defined by f(x) = x2 and g(x) = x + 1. Find formulas for f ∘ g and g ∘ f, and use them to explain why function composition is not generally commutative.

1.7 Injective, surjective and bijective functions

The following properties describe how the domain and codomain are connected.

Definition 1.29 (Injective, surjective and bijective). Let f : A → B.

  • The function is injective if, for all x1,x2 ∈ A,

    f(x1) = f(x2)⟹x1 = x2.
  • The function is surjective if f(A) = B. Equivalently, for every y ∈ B, there exists x ∈ A such that f(x) = y.
  • The function is bijective if it is both injective and surjective.

The terms “one-to-one” and “onto” are also used for injective and surjective, respectively.

Injectivity says that two different inputs cannot produce the same output. Surjectivity says that every member of the specified codomain is reached. Both properties depend on the full function specification, not only on its formula.

Example 1.30 (The same rule with different domains and codomains). Consider three functions, each with the rule x↦x2.

  1. The function f1 : ℝ → ℝ is not injective because f1(1) = f1(−1), and it is not surjective because no negative real number is a square.
  2. The function f2 : ℝ → [0,∞) is surjective, because every y ≥ 0 equals (y)2, but it is not injective.
  3. The function f3 : [0,∞) → [0,∞) is injective and surjective, so it is bijective.

The example shows separately how restricting the codomain can create surjectivity and how restricting the domain can create injectivity.

Definition 1.31 (Inverse function). Let f : A → B. A function g : B → A is an inverse function of f if

g(f(x)) = xfor every x ∈ A,

and

f(g(y)) = yfor every y ∈ B.

An inverse function, when it exists, is unique. If g and h are both inverse functions of f, then for every y ∈ B,

g(y) = g(f(h(y))) = h(y).

The first line uses f(h(y)) = y, and the second uses g(f(x)) = x with x = h(y). We therefore write the inverse function as f−1 : B → A.

For the bijective function f3 in the preceding example, f3−1(y) = y. This inverse function is not the reciprocal 1∕f3(y).

Proposition 1.32. A function has an inverse function if and only if it is bijective.

Proof. Suppose first that f : A → B is bijective. Surjectivity says that for every y ∈ B there is at least one x ∈ A with f(x) = y. Injectivity says that this x is unique. We may therefore define f−1(y) to be this unique x, and the two inverse identities follow.

Conversely, suppose an inverse function f−1 : B → A exists. If f(x1) = f(x2), applying f−1 to the common value gives

f−1(f(x 1)) = f−1(f(x 2)) x1 = x2.

Thus f is injective. For every y ∈ B, the element x = f−1(y) satisfies f(x) = y, so f is surjective. Hence f is bijective. □

Order properties of a function give a convenient way to establish injectivity.

Definition 1.33 (Monotone functions). Let f : D → ℝ, where D ⊆ ℝ, and let E ⊆ D. The function f is

  • non-decreasing on E if f(x) ≤ f(y) whenever x,y ∈ E and x < y;
  • strictly increasing on E if f(x) < f(y) whenever x,y ∈ E and x < y;
  • non-increasing on E if f(x) ≥ f(y) whenever x,y ∈ E and x < y;
  • strictly decreasing on E if f(x) > f(y) whenever x,y ∈ E and x < y.

The function is monotone on E if it is non-decreasing or non-increasing there, and strictly monotone if it is strictly increasing or strictly decreasing there.

A strictly monotone function is injective on E: if x,y ∈ E and x < y, then f(x)≠f(y). For example, x↦x2 is strictly increasing on [0,∞), and hence injective there, but it is not monotone on ℝ.

1.8 Elementary functions and their natural domains

The following familiar families will be used throughout the course. At this stage our purpose is to standardise their notation and domains, not to derive all of their properties.

  • A polynomial, such as p(x) = 3x2 − 2x + 1, has natural domain ℝ.
  • A rational function P(x)∕Q(x) is defined where Q(x)≠0.
  • The domain of a power or root must be stated carefully. For example, x has real domain [0,∞), whereas x−1 has domain ℝ ∖{0}.
  • For a fixed base b > 0, the exponential function bx has domain ℝ and positive image. The most important base is Euler’s number e ≈ 2.718, and ex is also written exp⁡x.
  • The natural logarithm log⁡x has domain (0,∞). It is the inverse function of exp⁡ : ℝ → (0,∞), so log⁡(ex) = x for every real x and elog⁡x = x for every x > 0.
  • The functions sin⁡x and cos⁡x have domain ℝ. The functions tan⁡x = sin⁡x∕cos⁡x and sec⁡x = 1∕cos⁡x are defined where cos⁡x≠0.

We shall also use the following standard monotonicity facts without proof: x2 and x are strictly increasing on [0,∞); for b > 1, the exponential bx is strictly increasing on ℝ; and log⁡x is strictly increasing on (0,∞). The hyperbolic functions, which are built from ex and e−x, are introduced in Chapter 11.

Whenever an expression contains several operations, all domain restrictions must hold simultaneously. For example, the natural domain of

h(x) = x − 1 x − 2

is [1,∞) ∖{2}: the square root requires x ≥ 1, and the denominator requires x≠2.

Example 1.34 (A punctured natural domain). Consider the function

f(x) = x2 − 1 x − 1 .

For x≠1 it simplifies to g(x) = x + 1, and g has natural domain ℝ. Even so, f(x) = g(x) only for x≠1: the original formula is not defined at x = 1, so 1 cannot be added to the domain of f. The natural domain of f remains ℝ ∖{1}, which we call a punctured domain.

1.9 Finite, countably infinite and countable sets

Some infinite sets can be listed in an ordered sequence without missing an element. The relevant definition uses the functions developed above.

Definition 1.35 (Countability). A set A is countably infinite if there is a bijection

f : ℕ → A.

A set is countable if it is finite or countably infinite.

Thus “countable” includes finite sets in this course. When infinitude matters, we shall say “countably infinite” explicitly.

The set ℕ is countably infinite because the identity function is a bijection from ℕ to itself. More surprisingly, the integers are also countably infinite, even though they extend without end in two directions.

Proposition 1.36. The set ℤ is countably infinite.

Proof. The list

0,1,−1,2,−2,3,−3,…

suggests the function ϕ : ℕ → ℤ defined by

ϕ(n) = { 0, n = 0, n + 1 2 ,n is odd, −n 2, n ≥ 2 is even.

Define ψ : ℤ → ℕ by

ψ(z) = { 2z − 1,z > 0, −2z, z ≤ 0.

If z > 0, then ψ(z) is odd and ϕ(ψ(z)) = z. If z ≤ 0, then ψ(z) is even and ϕ(ψ(z)) = z. Checking the even and odd cases similarly gives ψ(ϕ(n)) = n for every n ∈ ℕ. Thus ψ is the inverse of ϕ, so ϕ is a bijection. □

Figure 1.5 shows the first few values of ϕ. Alternating positive and negative integers ensures that no integer is omitted or repeated.

Remark 1.37 (The rational numbers). The set ℚ is also countably infinite. One can arrange fractions with integer numerators and positive denominators in a grid, traverse the grid diagonally, and omit repetitions such as 1∕2 = 2∕4. Turning that picture into a careful bijection requires accounting for signs and repeated representations; the diagonal arrangement gives the main idea.

Not every infinite set is countable. A set that is not countable is called uncountable.

Theorem 1.38 (The real numbers are uncountable). The set ℝ is uncountable.

We state this theorem without proof. The standard argument, due to Cantor, supposes that the real numbers in (0,1) have been listed as x0,x1,x2,… using their decimal expansions. It then constructs a number in (0,1) whose (n + 1)th decimal digit differs from the (n + 1)th decimal digit of xn, for every n ∈ ℕ. This number differs from every listed number, so no list indexed by ℕ can contain every real number. Making the construction precise requires care with numbers that have two decimal expansions, such as 0.1999… = 0.2. Thus ℕ, ℤ and ℚ are countably infinite, whereas ℝ is not.

Exercise 1.39 (Functions and countability). Let f : ℝ → ℝ be defined by f(x) = 2x − 3.

  1. Find f([0,2]) and f−1([1,5]).
  2. Decide whether f is injective, surjective or bijective.
  3. If an inverse exists, find its rule and state its domain and codomain.
  4. Explain why the function n↦2n is a bijection from ℕ to the set of non-negative even integers.

The function viewpoint has one further use. A real sequence is a function whose inputs are integer indices. This observation will let us distinguish the order of the terms from the set of values they happen to take.

Chapter 2
Sequences and Convergence

A sequence may appear to be merely a list, but regarding it as a function makes its structure precise. It also prepares us to express the idea that its terms get arbitrarily close to a real number, which we will later formalise as limits.

2.1 Sequences as indexed objects

Definition 2.1 (Real sequence). A real sequence indexed by ℕ is a function

a : ℕ → ℝ.

We normally write an instead of a(n) and denote the sequence by (an)n∈ℕ. If the first allowed index is n0, we write (an)n≥n0.

Order and repetition are part of a sequence. For example, the sequence defined by an = (−1)n for n ∈ ℕ is

(1,−1,1,−1,…),

whereas its set of values is only

{an : n ∈ ℕ} = {−1,1}.

The parentheses describe a sequence; braces describe a set.

2.2 The epsilon–N definition

Consider 1,1∕2,1∕3,1∕4,…. Its terms never equal 0, but they seem to approach 0. The precise statement must say more than “the terms get close”: it must work for every positive tolerance, however small.

Definition 2.2 (Convergence of a sequence). Let (an)n∈ℕ be a real sequence and let L ∈ ℝ. We say that (an) converges to L if

∀ ⁡𝜀 > 0∃ ⁡N ∈ ℕ∀ ⁡n ≥ N : |an − L| < 𝜀. (2.1)

We then write

an → Las n →∞,

or

lim ⁡ n→∞an = L.

A sequence that does not converge to a finite real number is said to diverge.

The same definition applies to a sequence (an)n≥n0 that starts at another index, with the threshold N taken to satisfy N ≥ n0. The definitions and results about sequences below are used with the same convention.

In ordinary language, Definition 2.2 says: for every tolerance 𝜀 > 0, there is a threshold index N such that every term from that index onwards lies within distance 𝜀 of L.

The order of the quantifiers is essential:

∀ ⁡𝜀 > 0∃ ⁡N∀ ⁡n ≥ N.

The value of N may depend on the chosen 𝜀, but after N has been chosen the same threshold must work for every n ≥ N. The definition does not merely require infinitely many terms to be close to L.

Geometrically, |an − L| < 𝜀 means

L − 𝜀 < an < L + 𝜀.

Thus every horizontal band of radius 𝜀 around L must eventually contain the whole tail of the sequence. Finitely many initial terms may lie outside the band. Figure 2.1 illustrates one choice of 𝜀 for the sequence (1∕n)n∈ℤ+.

Example 2.3 (A constant sequence). Let an = c for every n ∈ ℕ, where c ∈ ℝ. Given any 𝜀 > 0, choose N = 0. For every n ≥ N,

|an − c| = |c − c| = 0 < 𝜀.

Therefore an → c.

2.3 Direct examples from the definition

A direct convergence proof has a recognisable structure. We begin with an arbitrary 𝜀 > 0, choose a threshold N in terms of 𝜀, and then verify the required estimate for every n ≥ N.

Example 2.4 (The fundamental reciprocal limit). For n ∈ ℤ+, we have

1 n → 0as n →∞. (2.2)

Proof. Let 𝜀 > 0. By the Archimedean property, choose N ∈ ℤ+ such that

N > 1 𝜀.

If n ≥ N, then taking reciprocals of positive numbers reverses the inequality, so

|1 n − 0| = 1 n ≤ 1 N < 𝜀.

This is exactly the estimate required by the definition, so 1∕n → 0. □

The discovery and verification parts of this proof should be distinguished. Working backwards from 1∕n < 𝜀 suggests the sufficient condition n > 1∕𝜀. The written proof then works forwards: it chooses such an N and verifies the estimate.

Example 2.5 (A second direct proof). For n ∈ ℤ+, let

an = 2n + 1 n .

We prove directly that an → 2.

Proof. Let 𝜀 > 0. Choose N ∈ ℤ+ with N > 1∕𝜀. For every n ≥ N, simplify the error before estimating it:

|an − 2| = |2n + 1 n − 2| = |1 n | = 1 n ≤ 1 N < 𝜀.

Therefore an → 2 by the definition of convergence. □

In both examples, the threshold changes when the tolerance changes. For instance, a proof may need a much larger N for 𝜀 = 10−6 than for 𝜀 = 10−1. This dependence is permitted and expected.

2.4 A bounded sequence that does not converge

The sequence ((−1)n)n∈ℕ never leaves the interval [−1,1], but it continues to alternate. Boundedness alone therefore cannot guarantee convergence.

Proposition 2.6. The sequence defined by an = (−1)n for n ∈ ℕ diverges.

Proof. Suppose, for a contradiction, that an → L for some L ∈ ℝ. Apply the definition with 𝜀 = 1∕2. There is an index N such that

|an − L| < 1 2

for every n ≥ N.

Choose an even index n ≥ N and an odd index m ≥ N. Then an = 1 and am = −1, so

|1 − L| < 1 2and|− 1 − L| < 1 2.

The triangle inequality now gives

2 = |1 − (−1)| = |(1 − L) + (L + 1)| ≤|1 − L| + |L + 1| < 1 2 + 1 2 = 1,

which is impossible. Hence no such L exists. □

This proof uses the phrase “for every n ≥ N” decisively: it lets us choose both a large even index and a large odd index. If the definition required only some large terms to be close to L, the argument would fail.

Remark 2.7 (Finite changes). Changing finitely many terms of a sequence does not change whether it converges or what its limit is. Indeed, once N is chosen beyond all the changed indices, the two sequences have exactly the same tail.

Exercise 2.8 (A direct epsilon–N proof). Use Definition 2.2 to prove each limit. In each proof, state a valid choice of N in terms of 𝜀 and verify the required inequality for every n ≥ N.

  1. For n ∈ ℕ,

    4 n + 2 → 0as n →∞.

  2. For n ∈ ℤ+,

    3n2 + n + 1 2n2 − 1 → 1 2as n →∞.

Direct proofs reveal what convergence means, but repeating them for every algebraic expression would be inefficient. We therefore turn the definition into a practical toolkit. We first establish two structural facts: a sequence cannot approach two different real numbers, and a convergent sequence cannot become arbitrarily large. We then prove rules for combining known limits.

2.5 Uniqueness and boundedness

Theorem 2.9 (Uniqueness of sequence limits). If an → L and an → M, then L = M.

Proof. Suppose, for a contradiction, that L≠M, and set

𝜀 = |L − M| 3 > 0.

Because an → L, there is N1 such that |an − L| < 𝜀 whenever n ≥ N1. Because an → M, there is N2 such that |an − M| < 𝜀 whenever n ≥ N2.

Choose n ≥ max ⁡ {N1,N2}. The triangle inequality gives

|L − M| = |(L − an) + (an − M)| ≤|L − an| + |an − M| < 2𝜀 = 2 3|L − M|,

which is impossible because |L − M| > 0. Hence L = M. □

Uniqueness justifies speaking of the limit of a convergent sequence.

Definition 2.10 (Bounded sequence). A real sequence (an)n∈ℕ is bounded if there exists M > 0 such that

|an|≤ M

for every n ∈ ℕ.

This says that the set of values of the sequence lies inside the interval [−M,M].

Theorem 2.11 (Convergence implies boundedness). Every convergent real sequence is bounded.

Proof. Suppose an → L. Apply the definition with 𝜀 = 1. There is an index N ≥ 1 such that

|an − L| < 1

whenever n ≥ N. For these tail terms, the triangle inequality gives

|an| = |(an − L) + L| ≤|an − L| + |L| < 1 + |L|.

Only the finitely many initial terms a0,…,aN−1 remain. Define

M = 1 + max ⁡ {|a0|,… ⁡ ,|aN−1|,|L|}.

Then M > 0 and |an|≤ M for every n ∈ ℕ. □

The converse is false: ((−1)n) is bounded but divergent. It is important to remember the direction

convergent⟹bounded,

not its reversal.

2.6 Algebra of sequence limits

Theorem 2.12 (Algebra of sequence limits). Suppose an → a and bn → b, and let c ∈ ℝ. Then

an + bn → a + b, can → 𝑐𝑎, anbn → 𝑎𝑏.

If b≠0 and bn≠0 eventually, then

an bn → a b.

Proof. We prove each rule from the definition.

For the sum, let 𝜀 > 0. Choose N1 such that |an − a| < 𝜀∕2 for n ≥ N1, and choose N2 such that |bn − b| < 𝜀∕2 for n ≥ N2. If n ≥ max ⁡ {N1,N2}, then

|(an + bn) − (a + b)| = |(an − a) + (bn − b)| ≤|an − a| + |bn − b| < 𝜀 2 + 𝜀 2 = 𝜀.

The two errors are each assigned half of the available tolerance.

For scalar multiplication, the case c = 0 is immediate. If c≠0, choose N such that |an − a| < 𝜀∕|c| whenever n ≥ N. Then

|can − 𝑐𝑎| = |c||an − a| < 𝜀.

For the product, convergence of (bn) implies that it is bounded, so choose M > 0 with |bn|≤ M for every n. Given 𝜀 > 0, choose N1 such that

|an − a| < 𝜀 2M

for n ≥ N1, and choose N2 such that

|bn − b| < 𝜀 2(|a| + 1)

for n ≥ N2. If n ≥ max ⁡ {N1,N2}, then adding and subtracting abn gives

|anbn − 𝑎𝑏| = |(an − a)bn + a(bn − b)| ≤|an − a||bn| + |a||bn − b| < 𝜀 2MM + 𝜀|a| 2(|a| + 1) < 𝜀 2 + 𝜀 2 = 𝜀.

For the quotient, we first prove that 1∕bn → 1∕b. Since bn → b≠0, there is N0 such that

|bn − b| < |b| 2

for n ≥ N0. The triangle inequality, rearranged as in the proof of Corollary 1.19, then gives

|b| ≤|b − bn| + |bn| |bn| ≥|b|−|bn − b| |bn| > |b| 2 .

Since |b|∕2 > 0, the terms bn are automatically non-zero for all sufficiently large n. Given 𝜀 > 0, also choose N1 so that

|bn − b| < 𝜀|b|2 2

for n ≥ N1. If n ≥ max ⁡ {N0,N1}, then

| 1 bn − 1 b | = |b − bn| |bn||b| ≤ 2|bn − b| |b|2 < 𝜀.

Hence 1∕bn → 1∕b. Applying the product rule to an(1∕bn) proves the quotient rule. □

The difference rule follows by combining the sum and scalar rules:

an − bn = an + (−1)bn → a − b.

The non-zero condition in the quotient rule is essential. For example, 1∕n → 0, but dividing the constant sequence 1 by 1∕n produces n, which does not have a finite limit.

Example 2.13 (A simple rational expression). For n ∈ ℤ+, using the constant, sum and scalar rules together with (2.2),

3n + 1 n = 3 + 1 n → 3 + 0 = 3.

Example 2.14 (Comparing highest powers). For n ≥ 2, the denominator below equals (n − 1)2≠0. To evaluate

lim ⁡ n→∞ 3n2 + n n2 − 2n + 1,

divide numerator and denominator by n2:

3n2 + n n2 − 2n + 1 = 3 + 1∕n 1 − 2∕n + 1∕n2 → 3 + 0 1 − 0 + 0 = 3.

The limiting denominator is 1, so the quotient rule applies. The calculation is justified by the limit laws; merely saying “keep the highest powers” would hide that justification.

Exercise 2.15 (A bounded factor and a null sequence). Suppose that (an)n∈ℕ is bounded and bn → 0. Prove directly from the definitions that

anbn → 0.

Explain why the algebra of sequence limits cannot be applied directly unless (an) is also known to converge.

2.7 Order and the Squeeze Theorem

An assertion about all sufficiently large indices is called an eventual assertion. For example, an ≤ bn eventually means that there is N0 such that an ≤ bn for every n ≥ N0.

Proposition 2.16 (Order preservation). Suppose an → a, bn → b, and an ≤ bn eventually. Then a ≤ b.

Proof. Suppose instead that a > b, and set 𝜀 = (a − b)∕3. For all sufficiently large n, convergence gives

an > a − 𝜀andbn < b + 𝜀.

Moreover,

(a − 𝜀) − (b + 𝜀) = a − b − 2𝜀 = a − b 3 > 0.

Therefore an > bn for all sufficiently large n, contradicting the eventual inequality an ≤ bn. Hence a ≤ b. □

Exercise 2.17 (Strict inequalities and limits). Suppose that an < bn for every n ∈ ℤ+ and that both sequences converge. Must

lim ⁡ n→∞an < lim ⁡ n→∞bn

hold? Prove the statement or give a counterexample, and explain why this does not contradict order preservation.

Order preservation compares two limits. When a sequence lies between two others having the same limit, we obtain a stronger conclusion.

Theorem 2.18 (Squeeze Theorem). Suppose that

an ≤ bn ≤ cn

eventually, and that an → L and cn → L. Then bn → L.

Proof. Let 𝜀 > 0. Since an → L, there is N1 such that

L − 𝜀 < an < L + 𝜀

whenever n ≥ N1. Since cn → L, there is N2 such that

L − 𝜀 < cn < L + 𝜀

whenever n ≥ N2. Let N0 be a threshold after which an ≤ bn ≤ cn holds.

If n ≥ max ⁡ {N0,N1,N2}, then

L − 𝜀 < an ≤ bn ≤ cn < L + 𝜀.

It follows that |bn − L| < 𝜀, so bn → L. □

Example 2.19 (Oscillation controlled by a shrinking factor). Although ((−1)n) diverges, the sequence ((−1)n∕n)n∈ℤ+ converges. Indeed,

−1 n ≤ (−1)n n ≤ 1 n

for every n ∈ ℤ+. Since both outer sequences tend to 0, the Squeeze Theorem gives

(−1)n n → 0.

The numerator keeps oscillating, but its possible size is forced into an interval whose width tends to zero. Figure 2.2 shows the alternating terms together with the two bounding sequences.

Remark 2.20 (A second Squeeze Theorem example). The same argument and the bound |sin⁡n|≤ 1 give, for n ∈ ℤ+,

sin⁡n n → 0.

This is another application of squeeze; no new trigonometric limit is required.

Exercise 2.21 (Sequence-limit consolidation). For n ∈ ℤ+, use the limit laws to evaluate

lim ⁡ n→∞2n2 − 3n + 4 5n2 + n .

Then use the Squeeze Theorem to prove

cos⁡n n2 → 0,n ∈ ℤ+.

State explicitly which bound on cos⁡n you use.

2.8 Divergence to infinity

A divergent sequence may fail to converge in different ways. The sequence ((−1)n) keeps oscillating inside a bounded interval, whereas the sequence (n) eventually exceeds every proposed level. The second behaviour has its own definition, obtained from Definition 2.2 by replacing the tolerance band around L with the region above an arbitrary level M.

Definition 2.22 (Divergence to ±∞). A real sequence (an)n∈ℕ diverges to + ∞ if

∀ ⁡M ∈ ℝ∃ ⁡N ∈ ℕ∀ ⁡n ≥ N : an > M.

We then write an → +∞ as n →∞, or lim ⁡ n→∞an = +∞. Similarly, (an) diverges to −∞ if

∀ ⁡M ∈ ℝ∃ ⁡N ∈ ℕ∀ ⁡n ≥ N : an < M.

The quantifier structure is the same as for convergence: the threshold N may depend on the level M, but it must then work for every later index. Since + ∞ and −∞ are not real numbers, a sequence that diverges to ±∞ does not converge. The notation lim ⁡ n→∞an = +∞ records how the sequence diverges; it does not assert that a real limit exists.

Example 2.23 (Two sequences that diverge to + ∞). For an = n, let M ∈ ℝ. The Archimedean property gives N ∈ ℕ with N > M, and then an = n ≥ N > M for every n ≥ N. Hence n → +∞.

For bn = n, let M ∈ ℝ. If M < 0, every term satisfies bn ≥ 0 > M, so N = 0 works. If M ≥ 0, choose N ∈ ℕ with N > M2. For every n ≥ N, the square root is strictly increasing on [0,∞), so

n ≥N > M2 = M.

Hence n → +∞, even though successive terms increase more and more slowly.

A sequence that diverges to + ∞ is not bounded above, but the converse is false. The sequence ((−1)nn)n∈ℕ is not bounded, yet it diverges neither to + ∞ nor to −∞: however large the index, its odd-indexed terms are negative and its even-indexed terms are non-negative.

Divergence to + ∞ is closely related to convergence to 0.

Proposition 2.24 (Reciprocals of sequences diverging to + ∞). If an → +∞, then an > 0 eventually and 1∕an → 0.

Proof. Taking M = 0 in Definition 2.22 shows that an > 0 for all sufficiently large n, so 1∕an is defined from some index onwards. Let 𝜀 > 0. Apply the definition with M = 1∕𝜀 to obtain N such that an > 1∕𝜀 for every n ≥ N. Taking reciprocals of positive numbers reverses the inequality, so

| 1 an − 0| = 1 an < 𝜀

for every n ≥ N. Hence 1∕an → 0. □

Example 2.25 (Geometric sequences). Let r ∈ ℝ and consider (rn)n∈ℕ. Suppose first that r > 1, and write r = 1 + d with d > 0. Every term in the binomial expansion of (1 + d)n is non-negative, so keeping only the first two terms gives

rn ≥ 1 + 𝑛𝑑.

Given M ∈ ℝ, the Archimedean property gives N ∈ ℕ with N > (M − 1)∕d. For every n ≥ N,

rn ≥ 1 + 𝑛𝑑 ≥ 1 + 𝑁𝑑 > M.

Hence rn → +∞.

Now suppose that 0 < |r| < 1. Then 1∕|r| > 1, so the first case gives (1∕|r|)n → +∞, and Proposition 2.24 gives |r|n → 0. Since |rn − 0| = |r|n, the definition of convergence shows that rn → 0 as well. The case r = 0 is immediate. For r = 1 the sequence is constant, and for r = −1 it is the divergent sequence ((−1)n). For r < −1, the terms alternate in sign while |rn|→ +∞, so the sequence diverges to neither + ∞ nor −∞.

Exercise 2.26 (Divergence to infinity).

  1. Use Definition 2.22 to prove that n2 − 3 → +∞ and that 5 − 2n →−∞.
  2. Suppose that an > 0 for every n ∈ ℕ and that an → 0. Prove that 1∕an → +∞.
  3. Suppose that an → +∞ and that (bn)n∈ℕ is bounded. Prove that an + bn → +∞.
  4. You may assume that sin⁡n > 1∕2 holds for infinitely many n ∈ ℕ, and that sin⁡n < −1∕2 also holds for infinitely many n. Use these facts to show that (nsin⁡n)n∈ℕ is not bounded above but does not diverge to + ∞.

We now have two complementary methods: the definition explains and proves convergence from first principles, while the limit laws and Squeeze Theorem handle larger expressions efficiently. We next transfer the same ideas from indexed terms an to values f(x) as a real variable x approaches a point.

Chapter 3
Function Limits and Continuity

For a sequence, the index moves through larger and larger integers. For a function limit, the input x instead moves through real values close to a specified point a. The central question is whether closeness of x to a forces f(x) to be close to one real number L.

3.1 Accumulation points and function limits

A limit near a can only carry information if the domain contains points other than a arbitrarily close to it.

Definition 3.1 (Accumulation point). Let D ⊆ ℝ. A real number a is an accumulation point of D if, for every δ > 0, there exists x ∈ D such that

0 < |x − a| < δ.

Every point of an open interval is an accumulation point of that interval. The number 0 is an accumulation point of ℝ ∖{0} even though it is not in that set. In contrast, 0 is not an accumulation point of {0,1} because there are no other domain points sufficiently close to it. Requiring an accumulation point prevents a limit definition with no nearby inputs from becoming vacuously true.

A function limit examines nearby domain points on either side of a, but not a itself. Figure 3.1 shows the input condition geometrically before we state the full output condition.

Definition 3.2 (Finite function limit). Let f : D → ℝ, let a be an accumulation point of D, and let L ∈ ℝ. We write

lim ⁡ x→af(x) = L

if

∀ ⁡𝜀 > 0∃ ⁡δ > 0∀ ⁡x ∈ D : 0 < |x − a| < δ⟹|f(x) − L| < 𝜀. (3.1)

The number 𝜀 controls the allowed output error, while δ controls the input distance. In ordinary language: for every output tolerance 𝜀 > 0, we can choose an input tolerance δ > 0 such that every domain point within distance δ of a, apart from a itself, has its output within distance 𝜀 of L.

As in sequence convergence, the choice of δ may depend on 𝜀. Once δ is chosen, however, it must work for every x ∈ D satisfying the input condition.

The condition

0 < |x − a|

excludes x = a. Consequently, the value f(a) is irrelevant to the punctured limit. The function need not even be defined at a. Figure 3.2 shows the two tolerances together.

3.2 Direct epsilon–delta calculations

The structure of an epsilon–delta proof mirrors that of an epsilon–N proof. We simplify the output error, determine a sufficient restriction on the input error, and then write the proof forwards.

Example 3.3. We prove directly that

lim ⁡ x→2(3x + 1) = 7.

Proof. Let 𝜀 > 0. We first simplify the output error:

|(3x + 1) − 7| = |3x − 6| = 3|x − 2|.

This calculation suggests choosing

δ = 𝜀 3.

If 0 < |x − 2| < δ, then

|(3x + 1) − 7| = 3|x − 2| < 3δ = 𝜀.

Therefore the required limit follows from Definition 3.2. □

The preliminary algebra explains how the choice of δ was discovered. The proof itself begins with an arbitrary 𝜀, makes the choice, and verifies that it works.

In that example the output error was a constant multiple of |x − 2|. More often, the output error is |x − a| times a second factor that still depends on x. The method is then to bound the second factor first, by agreeing to keep x within a fixed distance of a, and only afterwards to make |x − a| small.

It is also enough to find a suitable δ for every 𝜀 ∈ (0,1). If |f(x) − L| < 𝜀 whenever 0 < |x − a| < δ, then the same δ also works for every larger tolerance. For 𝜀 ≥ 1 we may therefore reuse the δ found for 𝜀 = 1∕2.

Example 3.4 (Bounding a varying factor). We prove directly that

lim ⁡ x→2x2 = 4.

Proof. We first simplify the output error:

|x2 − 4| = |x − 2||x + 2|.

The factor |x − 2| is controlled by δ, but |x + 2| varies with x. If |x − 2| < 1, then 1 < x < 3, so 3 < x + 2 < 5 and hence |x + 2| < 5. On this range |x2 − 4| < 5|x − 2|, which suggests choosing δ = 𝜀∕5.

Let 0 < 𝜀 < 1 and choose δ = 𝜀∕5. Then δ < 1. If 0 < |x − 2| < δ, then also |x − 2| < 1, so |x + 2| < 5 and

|x2 − 4| = |x − 2||x + 2| < 5δ = 𝜀.

By the observation before this example, this proves the limit. □

The restriction |x − 2| < 1 is a convenient choice, not a necessary one: another fixed distance would give a different constant in place of 5. Without the assumption 𝜀 < 1, the same argument works with δ = min ⁡ {1,𝜀∕5}, because the minimum keeps the restriction |x − 2| < 1 in force.

Theorem 3.5 (Uniqueness of function limits). Let f : D → ℝ, and let a be an accumulation point of D. If

lim ⁡ x→af(x) = Landlim ⁡ x→af(x) = M,

then L = M.

Proof. Suppose L≠M and set 𝜀 = |L − M|∕3. The first limit supplies δ1 > 0 such that |f(x) − L| < 𝜀 whenever 0 < |x − a| < δ1. The second supplies δ2 > 0 such that |f(x) − M| < 𝜀 whenever 0 < |x − a| < δ2.

Because a is an accumulation point, choose x ∈ D satisfying

0 < |x − a| < min ⁡ {δ1,δ2}.

The triangle inequality then gives

|L − M| ≤|L − f(x)| + |f(x) − M| < 2𝜀 = 2 3|L − M|,

which is impossible. Hence L = M. □

The accumulation-point hypothesis is used when we choose the nearby domain point x. This is precisely why it was included in the definition.

A two-sided limit allows the input to approach from either direction. Before developing algebraic rules for such limits, we separate the two possible directions of approach. This will let us diagnose examples in which no two-sided limit can exist.

3.3 One-sided limits

Sometimes the behaviour differs on the two sides of a point, so we record the directions separately.

Definition 3.6 (One-sided limits). Let f : D → ℝ, let a ∈ ℝ and let L ∈ ℝ.

  • Suppose that a is an accumulation point of D ∩ (−∞,a). We write lim ⁡ x→a−f(x) = L if, for every 𝜀 > 0, there exists δ > 0 such that

    a − δ < x < aandx ∈ D

    imply |f(x) − L| < 𝜀. This is the left-hand limit.

  • Suppose that a is an accumulation point of D ∩ (a,∞). We write lim ⁡ x→a+f(x) = L if, for every 𝜀 > 0, there exists δ > 0 such that

    a < x < a + δandx ∈ D

    imply |f(x) − L| < 𝜀. This is the right-hand limit.

The accumulation conditions guarantee domain points arbitrarily close to a on the relevant side, so that a one-sided limit cannot hold vacuously.

Theorem 3.7 (Two-sided limit criterion). Let f : D → ℝ, and suppose that a is an accumulation point of both D ∩ (−∞,a) and D ∩ (a,∞). Then

lim ⁡ x→af(x) = L

if and only if

lim ⁡ x→a−f(x) = Landlim ⁡ x→a+f(x) = L.

Proof. If the two-sided limit equals L, restricting its defining implication to x < a proves the left-hand limit, and restricting it to x > a proves the right-hand limit.

Conversely, suppose both one-sided limits equal L. Given 𝜀 > 0, let δ− > 0 work on the left and let δ+ > 0 work on the right. Set

δ = min ⁡ {δ−,δ+}.

If 0 < |x − a| < δ, then either x < a or x > a. The appropriate one-sided definition gives |f(x) − L| < 𝜀 in either case. This is the two-sided limit definition. □

Example 3.8 (Disagreement of one-sided limits). Define f : ℝ ∖{0}→ ℝ by

f(x) = |x| x .

If x < 0, then |x| = −x and f(x) = −1. If x > 0, then |x| = x and f(x) = 1. Therefore

lim ⁡ x→0−f(x) = −1andlim ⁡ x→0+f(x) = 1.

The one-sided limits disagree, so the two-sided limit does not exist. The two horizontal pieces in Figure 3.3 make this disagreement visible.

Exercise 3.9 (A limit need not determine the point value). Decide whether the following statement is true: if

lim ⁡ x→a−f(x) = lim ⁡ x→a+f(x) = L,

then f(a) = L. Prove the statement or give a counterexample. State the additional condition that would make the conclusion valid.

When a two-sided limit does exist, its algebra can be developed by the same error estimates used for sequences.

3.4 Algebra of finite function limits

The sequence limit laws have direct analogues for functions.

Proposition 3.10 (Local boundedness). Let f : D → ℝ, and let a be an accumulation point of D. If lim ⁡ x→af(x) = A, then there are numbers δ0 > 0 and M > 0 such that

|f(x)|≤ M

whenever x ∈ D and 0 < |x − a| < δ0.

Proof. Use the limit definition with 𝜀 = 1. There is δ0 > 0 such that |f(x) − A| < 1 whenever 0 < |x − a| < δ0. For such x, the triangle inequality gives

|f(x)| ≤|f(x) − A| + |A| < 1 + |A|.

Thus, for example, M = 1 + |A| is a local bound. □

Theorem 3.11 (Algebra of finite function limits). Let f,g : D → ℝ, let a be an accumulation point of D, and suppose

lim ⁡ x→af(x) = Aandlim ⁡ x→ag(x) = B.

For every c ∈ ℝ,

lim ⁡ x→a(f(x) + g(x)) = A + B, lim ⁡ x→a𝑐𝑓(x) = 𝑐𝐴, lim ⁡ x→af(x)g(x) = 𝐴𝐵.

If B≠0, then g(x)≠0 for all sufficiently close punctured domain points, and

lim ⁡ x→af(x) g(x) = A B.

Proof. For the sum, let 𝜀 > 0. Choose δ1 > 0 such that |f(x) − A| < 𝜀∕2 when 0 < |x − a| < δ1, and choose δ2 > 0 similarly for |g(x) − B|. With δ = min ⁡ {δ1,δ2},

|(f(x) + g(x)) − (A + B)| ≤|f(x) − A| + |g(x) − B| < 𝜀 2 + 𝜀 2 = 𝜀

whenever 0 < |x − a| < δ.

The scalar rule follows in the same way from

|𝑐𝑓(x) − 𝑐𝐴| = |c||f(x) − A|,

using δ for the tolerance 𝜀∕|c| when c≠0; the case c = 0 is immediate.

For the product, local boundedness gives δ0 > 0 and M > 0 such that |g(x)|≤ M whenever 0 < |x − a| < δ0. Choose δ1 so that

|f(x) − A| < 𝜀 2M

when 0 < |x − a| < δ1, and choose δ2 so that

|g(x) − B| < 𝜀 2(|A| + 1)

when 0 < |x − a| < δ2. For 0 < |x − a| < min ⁡ {δ0,δ1,δ2},

|f(x)g(x) − 𝐴𝐵| = |(f(x) − A)g(x) + A(g(x) − B)| ≤|f(x) − A||g(x)| + |A||g(x) − B| < 𝜀 2 + 𝜀 2 = 𝜀.

For the quotient, the reverse triangle inequality (Corollary 1.19) shows that |g(x)| > |B|∕2 whenever |g(x) − B| < |B|∕2. Hence, sufficiently close to a,

| 1 g(x) − 1 B | = |B − g(x)| |g(x)||B| ≤ 2|g(x) − B| |B|2 .

Given 𝜀 > 0, requiring in addition that |g(x) − B| < 𝜀|B|2∕2 proves that 1∕g(x) → 1∕B. The quotient rule now follows from the product rule applied to f(x)(1∕g(x)). □

These proofs use exactly the same ideas as the sequence proofs. A maximum of finitely many threshold indices is replaced by a minimum of finitely many positive input tolerances.

3.5 Justified substitution

For the identity function, choosing δ = 𝜀 gives

lim ⁡ x→ax = a.

Constant functions also have their constant value as their limit. Repeated application of the algebraic limit laws therefore gives the following result.

Proposition 3.12 (Polynomial and rational substitution). If p is a polynomial, then

lim ⁡ x→ap(x) = p(a).

If p and q are polynomials and q(a)≠0, then

lim ⁡ x→ap(x) q(x) = p(a) q(a).

This is the first rigorous justification for direct substitution. The condition q(a)≠0 is part of the result and must be checked.

Example 3.13 (Routine substitution). Because the limiting denominator is non-zero,

lim ⁡ x→−2x3 + 2x2 − 1 5 − 3x = (−2)3 + 2(−2)2 − 1 5 − 3(−2) = − 8 + 8 − 1 11 = − 1 11.

The first line uses polynomial substitution and the quotient limit law. The remaining lines perform arithmetic.

Example 3.14 (Cancelling a common factor before taking a limit). Direct substitution into

x2 − 1 x − 1

at x = 1 produces 0∕0, so the quotient rule does not apply. However, for x≠1 we may factor and cancel:

x2 − 1 x − 1 = (x − 1)(x + 1) x − 1 = x + 1.

Since the following limit only considers x near 1 but not equal to 1, we may replace the original fraction with the simpler expression:

lim ⁡ x→1x2 − 1 x − 1 = lim ⁡ x→1(x + 1) = 2.

Note that cancellation does not define the original fraction at x = 1; it produces an equal expression only on the punctured domain, which is exactly what the limit needs.

Remark 3.15 (What a punctured limit ignores). The preceding removable limit would still equal 2 if the function were assigned any value at x = 1. A punctured limit records nearby behaviour, not the value at the limiting point. Continuity will impose the extra requirement that these two values agree.

Exercise 3.16 (Function limits).

  1. Prove directly from the epsilon–delta definition that

    lim ⁡ x→−1(2x − 5) = −7.

  2. Evaluate

    lim ⁡ x→3x2 − 9 x − 3 ,

    and explain why cancellation is legitimate for the limit.

  3. Let h(x) = 0 for x < 2 and h(x) = 1 for x > 2. Find the two one-sided limits at 2 and decide whether the two-sided limit exists.

  4. Prove directly from the one-sided epsilon–delta definition that

    lim ⁡ x→2− 1 1 − x = −1.

Function limits deliberately ignore the value at the point. Continuity combines the nearby behaviour with the actual value of the function. To make the idea that small input changes produce small output changes precise, we again use epsilon and delta rather than relying on a graph.

3.6 Epsilon–delta continuity and function limits

Definition 3.17 (Epsilon–delta continuity). Let f : D → ℝ and let a ∈ D. The function f is continuous at a if

∀ ⁡𝜀 > 0∃ ⁡δ > 0∀ ⁡x ∈ D : |x − a| < δ⟹|f(x) − f(a)| < 𝜀. (3.2)

If E ⊆ D, then f is continuous on E if it is continuous at every point of E.

This is the primary definition of continuity in the course. For every allowed output tolerance 𝜀, we must find an input tolerance δ that works for every domain point x sufficiently close to a.

Compare (3.2) with the function-limit definition (3.1). A punctured limit assumes

0 < |x − a| < δ

and compares f(x) with a proposed value L. Continuity assumes only

|x − a| < δ

and compares f(x) with the actual value f(a). The case x = a causes no difficulty because |f(a) − f(a)| = 0.

Proposition 3.18 (Continuity and the punctured limit). Let f : D → ℝ, and let a ∈ D be an accumulation point of D. Then

f is continuous at a⟺lim ⁡ x→af(x) = f(a).

Proof. Suppose first that f is continuous at a. Given 𝜀 > 0, continuity supplies δ > 0 such that |x − a| < δ implies |f(x) − f(a)| < 𝜀. The same implication remains true after adding the restriction 0 < |x − a|, so the punctured limit is f(a).

Conversely, suppose lim ⁡ x→af(x) = f(a). Given 𝜀 > 0, choose δ > 0 from the limit definition. If x ∈ D and |x − a| < δ, there are two cases. If x≠a, the punctured limit gives |f(x) − f(a)| < 𝜀. If x = a, then

|f(x) − f(a)| = 0 < 𝜀.

Thus the epsilon–delta definition of continuity holds. □

The proposition separates three requirements. First, the function must be defined at a. Second, the punctured limit

lim ⁡ x→af(x)

must exist. Finally, that limit must equal f(a).

Example 3.19 (A polynomial). Let p : ℝ → ℝ be defined by

p(x) = x3 − 2x + 4.

Polynomial substitution gives, for every a ∈ ℝ,

lim ⁡ x→ap(x) = p(a).

Therefore p is continuous on ℝ. For example,

lim ⁡ x→2p(x) = p(2) = 23 − 2(2) + 4 = 8.

The first line uses continuity; the remaining lines evaluate the function.

Exercise 3.20 (Continuity preserves strict positivity locally). Let f : D → ℝ be continuous at a ∈ D, and suppose that f(a) > 0. Use the epsilon–delta definition of continuity to prove that there exists δ > 0 such that

f(x) > f(a) 2 ,

for every x ∈ D satisfying |x − a| < δ.

3.7 The sequential characterisation

Continuity connects naturally with the sequence convergence developed earlier. If every sequence of inputs approaches a, continuity should force the corresponding sequence of outputs to approach f(a).

Theorem 3.21 (Sequential characterisation of continuity). Let f : D → ℝ and let a ∈ D. The function f is continuous at a if and only if, for every sequence (xn)n∈ℕ in D satisfying xn → a, we have

f(xn) → f(a).

We now prove the direction from epsilon–delta continuity to sequential continuity. The converse is deliberately reserved for the exercise immediately afterwards.

Proof that epsilon–delta continuity implies sequential continuity. Assume that f is continuous at a, and let (xn)n∈ℕ be any sequence in D such that xn → a.

Let 𝜀 > 0. By continuity of f at a, there exists δ > 0 such that, for every x ∈ D,

|x − a| < δ⟹|f(x) − f(a)| < 𝜀.

Because xn → a, the definition of sequence convergence supplies N ∈ ℕ such that

|xn − a| < δ

for every n ≥ N. Since every xn lies in D, continuity now gives

|f(xn) − f(a)| < 𝜀

for every n ≥ N. This is the definition of f(xn) → f(a). □

The proof uses continuity first to turn the requested output tolerance 𝜀 into an input tolerance δ. It then uses sequence convergence to turn that δ into a threshold index N.

Exercise 3.22 (Sequential continuity implies epsilon–delta continuity). Assume that for every sequence (xn)n∈ℕ in D with xn → a, we have f(xn) → f(a). Prove that f is epsilon–delta continuous at a by following these steps.

  1. Suppose, for a contradiction, that epsilon–delta continuity fails. Negate Definition 3.17 carefully to show that there is a fixed 𝜀0 > 0 such that, for every δ > 0, there exists x ∈ D satisfying

    |x − a| < δand|f(x) − f(a)|≥ 𝜀0.

  2. Set x0 = a. For each n ∈ ℤ+, apply this statement with δ = 1∕n to choose xn ∈ D such that

    |xn − a| < 1 nand|f(xn) − f(a)|≥ 𝜀0.
  3. Use the Squeeze Theorem to show that xn → a, and use the fixed lower bound 𝜀0 to show that f(xn)↛f(a).
  4. Explain why this contradicts the assumed sequential property, and conclude that f is epsilon–delta continuous at a.

This exercise is the converse direction of the sequential characterisation. It is not being used to redefine continuity: the epsilon–delta statement remains the primary definition.

To disprove continuity with sequences, the quantifier “every” is helpful. A single sequence xn → a for which f(xn)↛f(a) is enough to show that f is not continuous at a.

3.8 Algebra and composition of continuous functions

The limit laws now become rules for building continuous functions from simpler ones.

Theorem 3.23 (Algebra of continuous functions). Suppose f,g : D → ℝ are continuous at a ∈ D, and let c ∈ ℝ. Then f + g, 𝑐𝑓 and 𝑓𝑔 are continuous at a. If g(a)≠0, then the quotient f∕g, with domain {x ∈ D : g(x)≠0}, is continuous at a.

Proof. If a is an accumulation point of D, continuity gives

lim ⁡ x→af(x) = f(a)andlim ⁡ x→ag(x) = g(a).

The algebra of function limits then gives, for example,

lim ⁡ x→af(x)g(x) = (lim ⁡ x→af(x)) (lim ⁡ x→ag(x)) = f(a)g(a).

Thus 𝑓𝑔 is continuous at a. The sum and scalar rules follow in the same way. When g(a)≠0, the quotient limit law gives

lim ⁡ x→af(x) g(x) = f(a) g(a).

If a is not an accumulation point, there is a δ > 0 for which the only possible domain point satisfying |x − a| < δ is a itself. All the required continuity estimates are then immediate. □

Composition requires two continuity statements at two related points.

Theorem 3.24 (Continuity of a composition). Let f : D → E and g : E → ℝ. If f is continuous at a ∈ D and g is continuous at f(a), then g ∘ f is continuous at a.

Proof. Let 𝜀 > 0. Since g is continuous at f(a), there exists η > 0 such that, for every y ∈ E,

|y − f(a)| < η⟹|g(y) − g(f(a))| < 𝜀.

We use η as the requested output tolerance for f. Since f is continuous at a, there exists δ > 0 such that, for every x ∈ D,

|x − a| < δ⟹|f(x) − f(a)| < η.

Combining the two implications gives

|x − a| < δ⟹|g(f(x)) − g(f(a))| < 𝜀.

This is continuity of g ∘ f at a. □

The intermediate tolerance η separates the two stages of the composition: x must be close enough to a to make f(x) close to f(a), and that closeness must be sufficient to control g.

The algebra and composition rules reduce many continuity questions to a collection of standard building blocks.

3.9 Continuity of elementary functions

Theorem 3.25 (Continuity of elementary functions). The standard elementary functions are continuous on their natural domains. In particular, this applies to polynomials, rational functions away from zeros of their denominators, power and root functions where they are defined, the absolute-value function, exponential functions, logarithmic functions and trigonometric functions.

The construction of these functions and separate first-principles continuity proofs for every family are beyond the present scope. The theorem, together with the algebra and composition rules, is the practical justification for direct substitution into elementary functions whenever the limiting point belongs to the natural domain. For the absolute value, a direct proof is short: the reverse triangle inequality (Corollary 1.19) gives ||x|−|a|| ≤|x − a|, so δ = 𝜀 works.

Two further standard properties of continuous functions will be used later. Their proofs rely on the completeness of the real numbers and are left to later courses in analysis.

Theorem 3.26 (Extreme Value Theorem). Let a < b, and let f : [a,b] → ℝ be continuous. Then f is bounded, and there exist c,d ∈ [a,b] such that

f(c) ≤ f(x) ≤ f(d)for every x ∈ [a,b].

Thus a continuous function on a closed bounded interval attains a smallest value f(c) and a largest value f(d). Both hypotheses matter: x↦x is continuous on (0,1) but has no largest value there, and x↦1∕x is continuous on (0,1] but is not bounded.

Theorem 3.27 (Continuity of inverse functions). Let I be an interval, and let f : I → ℝ be continuous and strictly monotone. Then J = f(I) is an interval, f : I → J is a bijection, and its inverse function f−1 : J → I is continuous and strictly monotone.

For example, the restrictions of sine to [−π∕2,π∕2], of cosine to [0,π] and of tangent to (−π∕2,π∕2) are continuous and strictly monotone, so arcsin⁡, arccos⁡ and arctan⁡ are continuous. Applied to exp⁡, the theorem gives the continuity of log⁡ again.

Exercise 3.28 (Maximum and minimum of two continuous functions). Suppose that f,g : D → ℝ are continuous at a ∈ D. Use the continuity of the absolute-value function and the identities

max ⁡ {f(x),g(x)} = f(x) + g(x) + |f(x) − g(x)| 2 , min ⁡ {f(x),g(x)} = f(x) + g(x) −|f(x) − g(x)| 2 ,

to prove that the functions x↦max ⁡ {f(x),g(x)} and x↦min ⁡ {f(x),g(x)} are continuous at a.

Example 3.29 (A composition). The function

h(x) = log⁡(1 + x2)

is a composition of the polynomial 1 + x2, whose values are positive, and the natural logarithm. Both functions are continuous at the relevant points. Hence h is continuous on ℝ, and

lim ⁡ x→2 log⁡ ⁡ (1 + x2) = log⁡(1 + 22) = log⁡5.

3.10 Representative discontinuities

A function can fail one or more parts of the limit criterion for continuity. The examples below separate two common kinds of failure.

Example 3.30 (A removable discontinuity). Define f : ℝ → ℝ by

f(x) = { x2 − 1 x − 1 ,x≠1, 0, x = 1.

From the removable-limit calculation in the section on justified substitution,

lim ⁡ x→1f(x) = 2.

However, f(1) = 0, so

lim ⁡ x→1f(x)≠f(1).

Therefore f is not continuous at 1. If we replace the assigned value by f(1) = 2, then the limit and function value agree and the new function is continuous at 1. This is called a removable discontinuity because changing one function value removes it, as Figure 3.4 illustrates.

Example 3.31 (A jump discontinuity). Define j : ℝ → ℝ by

j(x) = { 0,x < 0, 1,x ≥ 0.

The one-sided limits are

lim ⁡ x→0−j(x) = 0andlim ⁡ x→0+j(x) = 1.

They disagree, so the two-sided limit does not exist and j is not continuous at 0. This is a jump discontinuity. Unlike the previous example, changing the single filled point cannot repair it, as Figure 3.5 shows.

The same failure can be detected by a sequence. Let

xn = (−1)n n + 1 ,n ∈ ℕ.

Since |xn| = 1∕(n + 1) → 0, we have xn → 0. When n is even, xn > 0 and j(xn) = 1; when n is odd, xn < 0 and j(xn) = 0. Thus (j(xn)) alternates between 1 and 0 and does not converge to j(0) = 1. This one counterexample sequence disproves continuity at 0; Figure 3.6 displays its alternating outputs.

Remark 3.32 (Common continuity errors). The existence of lim ⁡ x→af(x) is not enough for continuity: the limiting value must equal f(a). Conversely, a specified value f(a) cannot repair unequal one-sided limits. For a sequential proof of continuity, every sequence approaching a must work; for a sequential disproof, one counterexample sequence is enough.

Remark 3.33 (Continuity on a restricted domain). Continuity always uses points in the stated domain D. At an endpoint of a restricted domain, only domain points on the available side matter. For example, continuity of a function f : [0,∞) → ℝ at 0 is tested using x ≥ 0. Thus continuity is always relative to the stated domain.

Exercise 3.34 (Continuity). Let

f(x) = { x + 1,x < 1, c, x = 1, 3 − x,x > 1.
  1. Compute the left- and right-hand limits at 1.
  2. Determine the value of c for which f is continuous at 1.
  3. For any other value of c, construct a sequence xn → 1 that demonstrates the failure of sequential continuity.

3.11 Limits at infinity and infinite limits

Divergence to infinity for sequences has two analogues for functions. The input may grow without bound, or the output may grow without bound as the input approaches a point. Both situations occur repeatedly later in the course: in limits of quotients, in the behaviour of graphs far from the origin, and in integrals over unbounded intervals.

Definition 3.35 (Limits at infinity). Let f : D → ℝ, where D is not bounded above, and let L ∈ ℝ. We write

lim ⁡ x→∞f(x) = L

if

∀ ⁡𝜀 > 0∃ ⁡R ∈ ℝ∀ ⁡x ∈ D : x > R⟹|f(x) − L| < 𝜀.

If D is not bounded below, lim ⁡ x→−∞f(x) = L is defined by replacing the condition x > R with x < R.

The threshold R plays the role of the index threshold N for sequences. The requirement that D is not bounded above guarantees that there are domain points beyond every threshold, just as an accumulation point guarantees domain points arbitrarily close to a.

Definition 3.36 (Infinite limits). Let f : D → ℝ and let a be an accumulation point of D. We write

lim ⁡ x→af(x) = +∞

if

∀ ⁡M ∈ ℝ∃ ⁡δ > 0∀ ⁡x ∈ D : 0 < |x − a| < δ⟹f(x) > M.

The limit −∞ is defined by replacing f(x) > M with f(x) < M. One-sided infinite limits restrict x to a − δ < x < a or to a < x < a + δ, under the corresponding accumulation condition, as in the definition of one-sided limits. Finally, if D is not bounded above, lim ⁡ x→∞f(x) = +∞ means that for every M ∈ ℝ there exists R ∈ ℝ such that f(x) > M for every x ∈ D with x > R. The remaining combinations of signs are defined in the same way.

As for sequences, the statement lim ⁡ x→af(x) = +∞ describes a way in which f fails to have a finite limit at a. The algebra of finite function limits does not apply to such statements. It does apply to finite limits as x →∞ or x →−∞: the proofs carry over when each condition 0 < |x − a| < δ is replaced by a condition x > R or x < R, and each minimum of finitely many values of δ is replaced by the maximum or minimum of finitely many thresholds.

Example 3.37 (Reciprocals of powers). We first prove that

lim ⁡ x→∞1 x = 0.

Let 𝜀 > 0 and choose R = 1∕𝜀. If x > R, then x > 0, and taking reciprocals of positive numbers reverses the inequality:

|1 x − 0| = 1 x < 1 R = 𝜀.

Near 0, the function x↦1∕x2 instead becomes large. Given M ∈ ℝ, let K = max ⁡ {M,1} and δ = 1∕K. If 0 < |x| < δ, then 0 < x2 < 1∕K, and hence

1 x2 > K ≥ M.

Therefore lim ⁡ x→01∕x2 = +∞. Similar reasoning with δ = 1∕K, where K = max ⁡ {M,1} for the right-hand limit and K = max ⁡ {−M,1} for the left-hand limit, gives

lim ⁡ x→0+ 1 x = +∞andlim ⁡ x→0−1 x = −∞,

so 1∕x has neither a finite nor an infinite two-sided limit at 0.

Example 3.38 (A rational function at infinity). For x > 2, the denominator below is nonzero. Dividing numerator and denominator by x2 gives

3x2 + 2x − 1 x2 − 2 = 3 + 2∕x − 1∕x2 1 − 2∕x2 → 3 + 0 − 0 1 − 0 = 3

as x →∞. The second line uses 1∕x → 0 together with the product, sum and quotient laws for limits at infinity. The calculation mirrors Example 2.14 in Chapter 2.

We shall use the following standard facts about the exponential and logarithmic functions:

lim ⁡ x→∞ex = +∞, lim ⁡ x→−∞ex = 0, lim ⁡ x→∞log⁡ ⁡ x = +∞, lim ⁡ x→0+ log⁡ ⁡ x = −∞.

Also, lim ⁡ x→∞xp = +∞ for every fixed p > 0. The logarithmic limit at infinity illustrates the definition: given M ∈ ℝ, take R = eM. Since log⁡ is strictly increasing on (0,∞), every x > R satisfies log⁡x > log⁡R = M.

Continuity also allows a limit to be taken through an outer function. The proof has the same two-stage structure as the proof of continuity of a composition.

Proposition 3.39 (Limits through a continuous function). Let u : D → E and g : E → ℝ, where D is not bounded above. Suppose that

lim ⁡ x→∞u(x) = L,

where L ∈ E, and that g is continuous at L. Then

lim ⁡ x→∞g(u(x)) = g(L).

The same conclusion holds for limits as x →−∞, as x → a, and as x → a±, whenever the corresponding limit of u is L.

Proof. Let 𝜀 > 0. Continuity of g at L supplies η > 0 such that, for every y ∈ E,

|y − L| < η⟹|g(y) − g(L)| < 𝜀.

We use η as the requested tolerance for u. Definition 3.35 supplies R such that |u(x) − L| < η for every x ∈ D with x > R. For such x, taking y = u(x) gives |g(u(x)) − g(L)| < 𝜀. The other cases are proved in the same way, with the condition x > R replaced by the appropriate input condition. □

For example, 1∕x → 0 as x →∞ and the exponential function is continuous at 0, so e−1∕x → e0 = 1 as x →∞.

Exercise 3.40 (Limits involving infinity).

  1. Prove from Definition 3.35 that

    lim ⁡ x→∞2x + 1 x = 2.
  2. Prove from Definition 3.36 that lim ⁡ x→1+1∕(x − 1) = +∞, and state the corresponding left-hand limit.
  3. Suppose that lim ⁡ x→∞f(x) = +∞. Explain why 1∕f(x) is defined for all sufficiently large x, and prove that lim ⁡ x→∞1∕f(x) = 0.

  4. Evaluate

    lim ⁡ x→∞2x2 − x 5x2 + 3

    using the limit laws, and state where 1∕x → 0 is used.

  5. Use Proposition 3.39 to evaluate

    lim ⁡ x→∞cos⁡ ⁡ ( 𝜋𝑥 x + 1 ).
  6. Let f(x) = x + 1, g(x) = x and h(x) = x2. Each function tends to + ∞ as x →∞. Find the limits of f(x) − g(x), h(x) − g(x), f(x)∕g(x) and h(x)∕g(x) as x →∞. Explain why expressions such as ∞−∞ and ∞∕∞ are called indeterminate.

These foundations lead directly to differentiation. Chapter 4 studies the limiting behaviour of expressions of the form

f(a + h) − f(a) h ,h≠0,

as h → 0. The limit language developed here is what will make that investigation precise.
